# John 12:1–25: Research notes

**About these notes:** I ran out of search and fetch calls before I could cover everything. Parts of the full Enduring Word page were cut off, and I couldn't open the Bible Hub commentary pages for each verse. So vv. 10–11, 15–16 and 20–22 have only thin coverage. I found no Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist-site (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Pentecostal-site, Orthodox (oca.org) or NET Bible material on this passage, and no direct discussion of prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. The only real dispute between traditions I found is over who Mary was (v. 3). On the other verses the Protestant writers I read basically agree.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: "Six days before the Passover" starts Jesus' final week. Almost one-half of John's Gospel is given to this last week. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- On the timing: Matthew and Mark say "two days" and John says "six." The Catholic Encyclopedia argues there was only one anointing, because St. John does not necessarily mean that the supper and the anointing took place six days before, but only that Christ came to Bethany six days before the Passover. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09761a.htm
- Dods, quoted by Guzik: the other Gospels place the meal out of order so they can show what moved Judas to act. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/

**v. 2**
- Guzik says the dinner was probably to celebrate Lazarus being raised. Lazarus is named twice in vv. 1–2, and Maclaren takes that as a sign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Whose house was it? Matthew and Mark say Simon the leper's. Ligonier argues that since John links it to Lazarus and his sisters, Simon is likely a family member, probably the father of the siblings. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/anointing-of-jesus Guzik notes that some think Simon was a relative, or even Martha's husband. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Barclay's reasoning: where else would Martha be serving but in her own house? https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-5.html

**v. 3**
- *Traditional reading.* Guzik sees three kinds of devotion here: remarkable humility (anointing His feet, not His head), remarkable extremity (a pound of costly spikenard worth a year's wages), and remarkable unselfconsciousness in letting her hair down in public. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Barclay: "pistic" nard is a word no one really knows the meaning of. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-5.html
- Head or feet? Constable thinks probably she did both. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-3.html The Cambridge Bible says John records the less usual act (the feet) as evidence of her devotion. Gill reads the fragrance filling the house as a possible picture of the gospel's "sweet savour" spreading through the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/12-3.htm
- GotQuestions: by wiping his feet with her hair, Mary foreshadows Jesus' actions at the upcoming Last Supper when the Lord washes the disciples' feet. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jesus-anointed.html
- *Where traditions differ: who was Mary?*
  - Catholic: the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that most of the Latins hold that these three were one and the same (the "sinner" of Luke 7, Mary Magdalene and Mary of Bethany). It argues that John 11:2 supports this. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09761a.htm On Catholic Answers, a guest says this identification is the whole of the Western or Latin Christian tradition and that Gregory the Great made it explicit. https://www.catholic.com/audio/caf/was-jesus-too-harsh-to-martha
  - Baptist: Spurgeon says the woman in Luke 7 is not Mary of Bethany, and that the two accounts are distinct events. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-woman-which-was-a-sinner/ Desiring God traces the merging of these women to Gregory I's sermon of AD 591. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/who-do-you-say-that-she-was
  - Modern scholarship: Bible Odyssey says only John names her as Mary of Bethany, and that the Western church confused her with Mary Magdalene. https://saas.bibleodyssey.org/articles/mary-and-martha/
  - Modern criticism: Holtzmann called John's account a poor blend of Mark 14 and Luke 7. The Expositor's commentary rejects this as infelicitous criticism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/12-3.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Judas's betrayal looks darker beside Mary's devotion. This is the only evil act of Judas in the New Testament other than the betrayal, and even this one was done in secret. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Matthew Henry: Judas was not one of their nature, but only one of their number. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-3.html

**v. 5**
- 300 denarii was about a year's wages for a labourer. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/a-complete-waste/
- Matthew and Mark say "the disciples" objected, while John names Judas. Coffman explains this as Judas persuading the others to join him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-5.html
- *Note on misuse:* Guzik warns that the idea "nothing is too good for Jesus" can be twisted into a justification for all kinds of opulence and luxury for those who claim to serve him. He points out that the gift went directly to Jesus, in a single act. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/ (He doesn't name a movement.)

**v. 6**
- Ligonier: Judas's concern was invented. Greed drove him, not care for the poor. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/anointing-of-jesus
- Guzik cites Tasker on the Greek verb: it can mean both "carry" and "carry off," and Judas did both. Guzik adds that Jesus knew Judas was a thief and still made him treasurer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/

**v. 7**
- A debated verse. Piper calls it a very difficult verse. He reads it as Jesus telling Judas to back off so that Mary can carry on, including at his burial. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/leave-her-alone-judas-this-is-for-my-burial
- Did Mary keep some of the perfume back? Whiston thought so. Benson calls that "unnatural," and the Pulpit Commentary says it doesn't fit Matthew and Mark. Meyer, on the other hand, holds that she used only a portion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/12-3.htm
- Bruce, quoted by Guzik: why object to perfume poured on Jesus while he was alive, when it would have been used on his body anyway? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/

**v. 8**
- Barclay: the poor can be helped at any time, but this kindness to Jesus had to be done now. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-5.html
- Precept Austin points to Jesus' promise in Matthew 28:20 that he is with us always. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-12-commentary

**vv. 9–11**
- Guzik: the chief priests were mostly Sadducees, who denied resurrection, so a living Lazarus embarrassed them. Clarke asks how they could miss that the one who raised Lazarus could raise him again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/

**vv. 12–13**
- Palm branches had been a national symbol for first-century Judea, often tied to hopes for the Messiah. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/greeting-the-king Guzik says the crowd wanted a political conqueror. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Calvin: the palms were a sign of joy at receiving a new king. Gill gives the name Bethany as meaning "house of dates." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-13.html
- "Hosanna" comes from Psalm 118:25 and means "save now." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Bible.org's Deffinbaugh calls the entry a most dramatic and emphatic claim to be the Messiah. https://bible.org/seriespage/un-triumphal-entry-john-129-19

**vv. 14–15**
- Guzik: riding the donkey deliberately fulfilled Zechariah 9:9 and showed that Jesus' kingdom was spiritual, not military. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/

**v. 16**
- Matthew Henry: what is written helps us understand what happened, and what happened helps us understand what is written. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_012.cfm

**vv. 17–18**
- Matthew Henry: the Greek word *emartyrei* means the witnesses would have sworn to it under oath. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_012.cfm

**v. 19**
- Tasker, quoted by Guzik: the Pharisees' words were unconsciously prophetic, like those of Caiaphas. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/

**vv. 20–22**
- Morris, quoted by Guzik: Jesus took the Greeks' coming as a sign that he would now die for the whole world, Greeks included. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- The Bridgeway Bible Commentary sees the Greeks as firstfruits of a great Gentile harvest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-24.html

**v. 23**
- Guzik: Jesus had said twice before that his hour had not come (John 2:4, 7:6). He was glorified on the cross, not in the eyes of people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Precept Austin: "has come" is in the Greek perfect tense, meaning there is no going back. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-12-commentary

**v. 24**
- The traditions I found agree on this verse:
  - Calvin (Reformed): Christ compares his death to sowing, which looks like destruction but brings far greater increase. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-24.html
  - Clarke (Wesleyan/Methodist): the grain stands for Jesus, his death, his resurrection, and redemption bought for a lost world. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-24.html
  - Gill (Baptist): Christ's death was planned and voluntary, not an accident. Same page.
- Piper: Jesus would bear fruit, including the Greeks, but only by dying. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/if-a-grain-of-wheat-dies-it-bears-much-fruit
- Barclay links the verse to the saying "the blood of the martyrs was the seed of the Church." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/12-24.html
- Critical view: Thoma suggested John is putting Paul's ideas into Jesus' mouth. https://biblehub.com/john/12-24.htm

**v. 25**
- Guzik: hating your life "in this world" means holding it loosely, as pilgrims whose home is in heaven. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-12/
- Precept Austin connects this verse back to Mary, who "hated her life" through her extravagant gift. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-12-commentary
